# Profile: propagation

> Band conditions, grey line, beacons and DX spotting

**Stage:** 1.0

## What it installs

A live map showing the grey line and solar indices, two DX cluster clients, a sun clock, the VOACAP propagation engine with a graphical front end that makes its output readable, a monitor for the international beacon network, and grid-square tools in command-line and graphical form.

**Disk footprint:** Around 300 MB. pythonprop's cartopy, scipy and matplotlib stack is most of it, and hamclock-next is a source build against SDL2.

## Why these belong together

Every one of these answers the same question from a different angle: is the band open, and to where. They are grouped rather than spread through the mode profiles because they are genuinely optional — a station that works one local repeater needs none of it — and because most of them depend on web services, which makes this the first profile a low-bandwidth or offline station skips.
**The beacon monitor is the one to notice.** The NCDXF/IARU beacons transmit on a fixed three-minute rotation from known transmitters at known powers in known places, so listening to 14.100 and noting which callsigns you hear is a real measurement of your own antenna and receiver. No website substitutes for that.

## Packages (11)

[`hamclock-next`](../packages/hamclock-next.md), [`xdx`](../packages/xdx.md), [`flcluster`](../packages/flcluster.md), [`sunclock`](../packages/sunclock.md), [`voacapl`](../packages/voacapl.md), [`pythonprop`](../packages/pythonprop.md), [`ibp`](../packages/ibp.md), [`wwl`](../packages/wwl.md), [`qgrid`](../packages/qgrid.md), [`python3-pyhamtools`](../packages/python3-pyhamtools.md), [`twclock`](../packages/twclock.md)

## What it deliberately excludes

**`openhamclock`, which Q-006 chose as the default client and which cannot be installed yet.** It is a Node and Vite web application rather than the C++ program the original HamClock was, and it needs an `npm` backend this project does not have — see `docs/reference/source-build-gaps.md` #7. `hamclock-next` ships instead: a maintained SDL2 rewrite that carries the original author's copyright forward and that this engine can actually build. The substitution is stated rather than made quietly. Also excludes SPLAT!, which answers "what does the terrain do to this specific path" and lives in `antenna`.

## What you configure by hand afterward

**A DX cluster client needs a node address and your callsign**, and neither is chosen for you. **VOACAP needs a smoothed sunspot number** for the month you are asking about, which is itself a prediction you supply, and antenna descriptions if you want the answer to be about your station rather than about a default dipole — treating that default as your station is the commonest way to get a confidently wrong answer. HamClock's data backend defaults to `ohb.works`, a community-run service, and is user-configurable; nobody has yet run a client end to end against it, so confirm before relying on it. The beacon monitor is a schedule computation, so a system clock a minute out tells you confidently about the wrong beacon.
